newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean Kim declares support for finance reforms.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean Kim declares support for finance reforms.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Tuesday declared his support for sweeping financial reforms that would increase the independence of the central bank and curtail the authority of the Finance Ministry.

The reforms, proposed by the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform, were formally presented to Kim on Tuesday in a meeting attended by the finance minister and the heads of the central bank and the financial supervisory boards.
"I believe the commission proposals are substantial and are on the right track," the president said.
He said the proposals contained "long-pending but difficult issues".
The commission said its proposals were aimed at improving international competitiveness, establishing a user-oriented financial industry and building healthy financial institutions.
The 31-member commission, composed of bankers, business leaders and scholars, generally suggested giving more management autonomy to financial institutions and lifting various government regulations.

The commission said central bank autonomy was needed to stabilise prices because controlling inflation could conflict with government efforts to promote economic growth. The panel said the central bank should be given full authority to design and implement monetary and inflation policies.
"First of all, the central bank should be independent and its status should be enhanced so that it can implement monetary policy neutrally," he said.
But the bank must be fully aware of its duties, including its role in curbing inflation, he said.

The panel proposed the Monetary Board, which currently sets monetary policies, should be the highest decision-making body in the central bank. It recommended the central bank governor chair the Monetary Board.
The finance minister now heads the board and recommends to the president five of nine board members.
The commission proposed unifying the three financial watchdogs -- the Office of Bank Supervision, the Securities Supervisory Board and the Insurance Supervisory Board.
It said the unified financial supervisory board should be under the direct control of the prime minister and that the head of the new board should have ministerial rank.

Analysts said the commission's plan was aimed at limiting the finance ministry's functions to policy-making. They said the ministry's current involvement in policy execution exerted too much influence over the economy.
"Given the global trend towards lowering barriers within the financial industry, the commission's proposal for a unified financial watchdog agency is heading in the right direction," Kim said.

After much discussion, the panel finally decided to uphold the current four percent individual shareholding limit in Korean banks. But it said the limit could be raised to 10 percent under certain condition and with prior government approval.
Analysts said the complicated criteria would prevent big conglomerates, or chaebol, from owning banks, which was expected to delay mergers and acquisitions in the financial industry.
The finance ministry will review the proposals and submit implementing legislation to a special session of the National Assembly this month.
"I hope the finance minister will prepare the government's reform bills based on the proposals and discuss them with political parties," Kim said.
"I would like the finance minister to submit legislation to this coming parliamentary session for adoption," he said.
